utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Indah Susanti for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Representing Stojan Zupljanin, Aleksandar Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there is no reason to delay us, may the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, good morning to you. Before Mr. Zecevic continues, I remind you of your solemn declaration. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, let's take a look at P997. Tab 23. Mr. Tusevljak, this is a report dated the 27th of August. It's signed by Sasa Blagojevic, the person who submitted the report. Are you familiar with this person, Sasa Blagojevic, and if so, who was he?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him. He was an operative in the Security Services Centre. He worked on crime prevention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this a report about his visit to the public security station in Vlasenica? Did he go there on your instructions?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what was his task?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely what he wrote here. He went there to speak to the chief of the crime prevention department and to assess the situation in that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You, as chief of the crime prevention police in the Security Services Centre, did you send your inspectors to perform such visits in public security stations or, more precisely, crime prevention departments in public security stations? I'm speaking here of your line work.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the second half of 1992, in the fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did all the operatives in all cases receive the same or similar assignment like this one?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was their assignment. They were supposed to assess the situation in crime prevention departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 930D1. It's tab 155.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document dated the 28th of August, 1992, signed by CSB chief Zoran Cvijetic. The document was sent to the public security stations in the territory of the Security Services Centre. Could you first confirm whether this is the signature of Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Enclosed to this memo was the rules on disciplinary responsibility of employees of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic under conditions of a state of war and the rules and the form of IDs of authorised officials of Internal Affairs organs, and all employees in all public security stations were supposed to be informed about this. Do you remember these rules on disciplinary responsibility promulgated towards the end of August 1992 in the state of war?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether disciplinary responsibility of the employees of the MUP was made any harsher by these rules?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I heard the question, I heard the answer, but I confess I don't understand it. Could you expand on that for me, please, Mr. Zecevic. When you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- made any harsher by the rules. Could you get the witness to expand on that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just point out that's a leading question. "What change, if any, did this produce in the rules" is the proper question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, do you remember what were the changes in disciplinary responsibility envisaged by these rules on disciplinary responsibility in the state of war?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the discipline and the behaviour of a policeman in police stations had to be much stricter. This means that the envisaged sanctions were much harsher. So many misdemeanours that would normally be accompanied by removal to another post now became the misdemeanours that would be accompanied by the removal from the service, which means that those persons were fired from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any changes in the procedure pertaining to the disciplinary misdemeanours?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that. I don't remember the procedure and whether there were any changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether dead-lines to institute or complete disciplinary proceedings were changed by this rule book?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that. I really haven't had a chance to look at these rules for the past 18 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe there is ample evidence in the transcript already about the contents of this rule, and actual rule instruction is an exhibit in this case. However, at this point, if there's no objection, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D583, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to take a look at 122D1. It's tab 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, while we're waiting for the new document, I thought you said that the rules to which this letter that we have just admitted was already in evidence. Do you happen to have the exhibit number of the rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, in just one second I will provide you with that. May I continue, Your Honours, and I will provide the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Absolutely. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this is a document dated the 12th of September, 1992, signed by the chief of Security Services Centre Zoran Cvijetic. It's on the following page. The document was sent to the chiefs of public security stations. Can you first confirm whether this is the signature of Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document is dated some 15 days after the previous document. It comes about 15 days after the document that we just saw by which the new rule book during the state of war was sent to public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for Trial Chamber's information, it's 1D54. This is instruction on disciplinary responsibility during the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of this document we find the following: First the reference to the previous document by which the new rule book was sent on the 28th of August, and then it goes on as follows: "Among other things, this rule defines what constitutes minor and serious dereliction of duty in the condition of war, as well as the levels of emergency in the conducting of disciplinary proceedings. In spite of these obligations, a certain number of SJBs have not taken this problem seriously enough. The responsibility for this lies with the chiefs managing these SJBs, who are authorised to do so by certain rules." And then we find the instruction that the SJBs who have not done so yet are to analyse the potential involvement of employees in criminal acts and other forms of dereliction of duty as defined by the law and to inform by the 30th of September, 1992. And if there were no such cases, a memo to this effect was also supposed to be sent. Sir, do you remember whether on any of the collegium meetings in the Security Services Centre these issues were discussed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were discussions on the collegium meetings by the chiefs of the police departments. They spoke about the answers received from the police stations. I assume that the first request sent by the chief of the centre did not produce adequate response. And then in order to [Realtime transcript read in error "Municipal Board"] amplify and highlight the seriousness of this request, another request from the centre and the Ministry of the Interior, another dispatch, was sent 15 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, on page 7, line 1, we find "Serbian" or "Serb," while what I said was "CSBs." My question was whether you remember if any of those issues were discussed on any of the collegium meetings. So this is merely to correct the transcript. And I think that a part of your answer was not recorded properly. It says here on page 7, line 4, that you said: "I assume that the first request sent by the chief of the centre did not produce adequate responses," from the field. And then the "Municipal Board." I actually don't understand what it says here, so I would like you to repeat the answer but slowly. What was it that you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see from this document, this dispatch, there was a discussion at the collegium meetings in the Security Services Centre. The subject of the discussion were the responses received from public security stations. These responses were inadequate, and that is why the chief of the centre sent another memo 15 days later, so that the chiefs of public security stations would take their duties more seriously and discharge their tasks in a more responsible manner. And as we can see from this document, they were supposed to act upon the new rules on disciplinary responsibility. And if they still found among their employees policemen who had committed criminal offences or were held responsible in some other way for such offences, they were supposed to be removed from the service on the basis of the new rule book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to clarify this once more: In case that an employee of the Ministry of the Interior committed criminal offences, what proceedings would be instituted against him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A criminal report would be submitted to the competent prosecutor's office. His immediate superior, chief of the public security station, was supposed to suspend him and institute disciplinary proceedings against such an employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I propose to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There's something that I do not quite understand with this. What we saw in the previous document was that the chief of the CSB of Sarajevo forwarded these new rules, the new rule book that applied during war time, to all the SJBs under its jurisdiction, and then only 15 days later the same chief of CSB finds it necessary to send out a new dispatch to call for action because, as you say, the response wasn't satisfactory. Now, two weeks is quite a short span of time, so what happened? And was there some events in between that triggered this second attempt by Mr. Cvijetic to remind the SJBs of their duties? I would have thought that it would take longer time to discover that the actions which the SJBs were supposed to take could lead to the conclusion that SJBs weren't taking this seriously. I mean, you couldn't discover that in only two weeks, could you? So my question to you is whether there was any incident between the first and the second dispatch that triggered the second dispatch? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand the question. If in this memo we find the reference to the dispatch of the 25th of July, 1992, it means that on the 25th of July, 1992, a dispatch was sent requesting the removal of the employees who had committed criminal offences. This means that the centre chiefs were supposed to start doing this from the 25th of July onwards. It is very probable that they invoked the lack of the rules on disciplinary responsibility. So in this memo the chief of the centre references first the memo of the 25th of July; that's more than a month before that. And then on the 12th of September he highlights once again the duty of the chiefs of public security stations without giving them a dead-line. He merely states that they are supposed to deal with this problem in a more serious fashion, the employees who are still employed in the Ministry of the Interior and who had committed criminal offences. Which means that they could not work in the ministry anymore, are supposed to be removed from service as soon as possible in accordance with the law. So nothing happened. There was nothing that made this following dispatch -- there was nothing that caused the next dispatch to come so soon after the first dispatch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And that's what I did not quite understand, but let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not going to object to the admission of this document, but Mr. Cvijetic -- I'm obsessed by Mr. Cvijetic, obviously. Mr. Zecevic only asked the question "do you remember this" and never asked the actual question "did you see this document at the time." I don't want to have to waste time going back over this when I cross-examine, and I would be grateful if it could be made clear before the document is admitted in short whether the witness is actually saying he saw the document at the time. It may be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I suppose it is something that -- for tidiness that should have been asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But it struck me that the obvious connection between this and the previous exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honour, I'm not -- this is a general request that simply for each of these documents, which are not signed by this witness and on the face of it there's no good reason why he would have seen it at the time, it's important that each time Mr. Zecevic seeks the admission of such a document we know for certain whether the witness saw it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honours, but that is precisely why I asked the witness whether he recognises the signature of the chief of the CSB. If Mr. Cvijetic would have been available - he passed away - we would have called Mr. Cvijetic on the stand, but there is no other way we can introduce the documents by the chief of the CSB but through one of his employees.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, as I say, I perfectly understand and, as I say, I'm not objecting to the admission. I'm simply asking that each time the witness is asked whether he actually saw the document at the time, because clearly what was discussed is important, but so is whether he saw the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And as I did say in response to Ms. Korner's first intervention, for completeness, it's a question that could be asked, but I -- for myself, I would have thought that the witness's answers to the document would have been sufficient to explain his familiarity and therefore allow it in. But, as I said, for tidiness, you'd ask the necessary question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you see this document at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should have seen every one of these documents because I was a member of the collegium of the centre chief where the documents were drafted and then presented in the morning, but to remember every piece of paper from 18 or 19 years ago and claim that I saw it or didn't, that would be absurd that I should have such memory and such recollection. But when I see a document which is in front of me, I see that it's from the Security Services Centre and sent to police stations. It was discussed in the centre chief's collegium meetings in the morning and we had to report, for each department, which documents were sent on behalf of the chief of the Security Services Centre with his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we get the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: A slight question -- well, I don't know if it's a question of interpretation or what the witness intended to convey, but I fully understand and appreciate what the witness has said about the dealing with something that would have happened years ago and his explanation as to the ordinary practice, but the word that was used in response to the question was "I should have." Had he said "I would have," then the rest of that answer would fall perfectly into place. But I'm just wondering whether I am making too much out of the fact that what came over the English was his choice of "should" as opposed to "would have," because there would, in English, be a subtle difference in what is intended to be conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you understood the question of His Honour?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't understand. This is why I'm not sure what I was supposed to have said. The interpretation was wrong. I said that all these documents which I see now before me which were sent on behalf of the Security Services Centre chief, that is to say, which he signed, and it's obvious that his signature is here, they were all discussed and they were presented at the morning collegium meetings which we held with the Security Services Centre chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll have to make due with that. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May we have the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D584, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the witness 924D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is tab 177. Precisely in order to illustrate --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] No translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have a translation on the monitor. I'm not sure if you are missing something in your --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Well, It must have come in, because it wasn't there yesterday. It must have come in overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, I see -- I mean, I'm sorry, we shouldn't do this. I said to Mr. Zecevic no translation because I didn't have a translation in my binder. It wasn't -- it's one of the new documents, I think. I see there is a translation on the screen, so it must have been uploaded into e-court sometime between when we last looked at it and today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, does that mean that this is one of documents we didn't decide upon yet for their admission to the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honours, at this point. If you just bear with me one moment, please. Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a list of 12 documents which were pending translation as of yesterday which you haven't decided upon. This document is not on that list, but I can read the list just for the record, perhaps, so we have it in -- on the record. It refers -- so the documents which are pending translations as of 16th of June, yesterday, which are added to Defence 65 ter list and which were not decided by Your Honours are: Document 938D1, document 939D1, document 940D1, 941D1, 942D1, 943D1, 944D1, 945D1, 946D1, 947D1, 948D1, and 952D1. Therefore, this document has been -- has had the translation before and it was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Zecevic is quite right, because I've just seen that it is, in fact, one of the documents I'm looking at that we don't object to. Some how or other the translation didn't get into my binder, so I apologize for wasting the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak, this is a document dated the 28th of September, 1992, and I think that it is precisely the one that will explain and provide an answer to the question asked by Judge Harhoff awhile ago. This document was signed by the chief of station Malko Koroman, or somebody did it for him. It was addressed to the Romanija-Birac CSB and it says "reference your document number 01478/92 dated the 12th of September, 1992." Please have a look at the previous document which we looked at, 1D584, under tab 24, so that you could -- so that we could compare them. What is the number of that document and what is the date of that document? I'm talking about 1D584 under tab 24.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the response of the police station Pale to the document dated the 12th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read the number of the document and the date for us, the one that's under tab 24.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of the document is 01-478/92, dated the 12th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, have you seen this document before, the one we are looking at now, 924D1 under tab 177?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was sent to the chief of the police department. It says here "Drago," which means that I probably did not see it at the time because my name is not recorded. But this was standard. The department which received this document from the chief of centre also collected all the responses so that the chief of centre could then send the report, once it was amalgamated, to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say Drago, "it says here Drago," where do you see that? Can you please clarify that for me.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's handwritten by pencil in the upper right-hand corner of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And which Drago does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to Drago Borovcanin who was the chief of the police department at the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the sake of completeness of this issue, I would propose that this document be admitted into evidence as there are no objections from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D585, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please now see the document under tab 157, 933D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 23rd of September, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date on this document is the 23rd of September, 1992. It is signed by the chief of the CSB Zoran Cvijetic. It was addressed to the public security stations in the territory of this CSB. Can you confirm whether this is Mr. Cvijetic's signature?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen this document at the time, in 1992, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reason being that the chief of the centre has signed it again and this was discussed at our collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document deals with the issue of difficulties on roads and difficulties with communications equipment. Mr. Tusevljak, do you remember -- you said that this was discussed but do you remember who or what were the measures which were taken on the basis of this order and this document in terms of improving the dispatch system or improving the communications system in the territory of the Security Services Centre at Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see here that this type of communication was only requested in case of urgent information being transmitted, that is to say, informing police stations. And the improvement was only that in a way what I told you about on the previous days could be speeded up. Due to difficulties with communication and the lack of adequate communications equipment, the information we received or sent were many days late. And, of course, if you have urgent information or something that is current and you cannot forward it, if you lose time, then the information loses its value completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the third paragraph says "in order to submit information to the Public Security Station Ilidza, Hadzici, Rajlovac, Ilijas, and Vogosca, the fax machines of the Ilidza SJB will be used." Does this mean that dispatches would only be sent to the Ilidza SJB and then from the Ilidza SJB it would be -- I apologise. Can you tell us what this means, technically speaking? How were the dispatches communicated?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, the first question, Your Honours, should be whether he knows this. In fact, a witness from the CSB dealing with communications was actually called, and this document wasn't put to the witness who was in a position to deal with it. He has to lay the foundation for being able to deal with that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the witness confirmed that it was discussed at the collegium meeting. We didn't have this document when -- in our possession before and that is why we didn't show it to the Prosecutor's witness who were called for the communications. I'm just trying to establish the witness's knowledge about the problem that they were facing, and he already testified about that, and the ways how -- how the CSB tried to remedy the situation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me first ask you this, or ask you again: Are you familiar with this problem and the resolution which was adopted? Was that a resolution adopted at a collegium meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the problem and I know that we agreed at the collegium that in this way speedier communication would be achieved. And that means that if a dispatch was sent to Public Security Station Ilidza, or a report perhaps, then the duty was either for these other police stations, which are listed here, to come to the police station in Ilidza to get the report there or the Ilidza SJB would distribute the report or the dispatch to the listed police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the instruction from paragraph 4; however, it also says here that these copied information should be distributed by relay to the SJB. Can you explain to us what this expression "by relay" means?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that -- that the SJB Ilidza Police would take all dispatches which are addressed to Vogosca, Rajlovac, and Ilijas and then take them only to the Rajlovac Police Station. Rajlovac Police Station would take their dispatch, the one addressed to them, and then bring the others to Ilijas and Vogosca. Those from Vogosca had the obligation to carry the remaining one to Ilijas. And this was how the response was brought back as well. It means that dispatches were handed from hand to hand to police patrols who had their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, it's a bit unclear to me what the type of information was which should be communicated through all these means. Was it every dispatch that should be communicated immediately through all available fax machines or was there any attempt to give priority to certain kinds of information? I mean, I suppose that some types of information were more important than others. And if there was a difficulty in transmitting information from one station to another, I suppose that what you would wish to do is to make some sort of priority. But I don't see that here. This dispatch is only about the means of communication but says nothing about the contents of the information or the type of information. Did I understand this correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The territory of the Security Services Centre at the time was affected by war operations. On a daily basis, the areas which were under the control of the Security Services Centre were under attack. This is a period when perhaps 80 per cent of the policemen were involved in active combat operations. The front lines shifted on a daily basis and policemen got killed every day. This was mostly information that was needed in order to carry out defensive operations. That means that assistance was to be given to a certain territory which was defending itself, or they informed us about the number of policemen who had been killed or if anyone had been wounded, and the like. That was the sort of information that was urgent and that needed to be transmitted to the final user as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 933D1 shall be Exhibit 1D586.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us have a look at the next document. This is 931D1, tab 196. Mr. Tusevljak, this is a document dated the 31st of August, 1992. An order signed by the chief of the CSB Zoran Cvijetic but signed for him. Can you recognise whose signature this is?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is signed by Cedo Nogo, who was an inspector from the crime police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From the police department where?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police department of the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This order orders some of the relevant police stations to send to the Zvornik Public Security Station four policemen each, whereas Novo Sarajevo SJB is to send eight policemen to Zvornik. Do you remember that these employees were sent to the public security station in Zvornik at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what was the reason for this and what was their task over there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that an action of the Ministry of the Interior was carried out in Zvornik at the time. The task was disbanding and routing the Yellow Wasps, and the assistance from the Security Services Centre was requested at the time. And this is why there was this request for the said employees to report to the SJB Zvornik as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when this action relating to Zute Ose took place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date because I was not involved in this action so I cannot remember the exact date, but I think it was around the end of August or early September. I wouldn't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that the action in Zvornik was carried out on the 30th of July and 1st of August, would that make it easier for you to remember?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Zecevic, I pointed out yesterday that this witness's recollection and his connection between events was a matter of importance and he should not be led on any dates. And you've just done it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just trying to find out if I can refresh his memory. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, A, there should be an application if that's the case. Secondly, as I pointed out yesterday, and I made it very clear, we are querying how the witness comes by some of his knowledge and how he connects things together. And therefore he should not be led in the fashion or helped out in a fashion that Mr. Zecevic has just done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Standing on its own of course, Ms. Korner, you're perfectly correct. But I'm wondering -- I thought - and please correct me if I'm wrong - that the dates of these events were established otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I ask -- I'm not at all clear whether the witness actually doesn't speak some English because he has a great deal of dealings with internationals. But nonetheless, for these purposes, I'll ask him to take his earphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, could you please remove your headphones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honours, I think it's important if there's really serious argument that he leaves court, because my understanding is he does speak English. He's dealt with international prosecutors, apart from anything else. Your Honours, the point is this: We are going to be contending that this witness's ability to give evidence about just about everything under the sun is a matter that we're going to be cross-examining on. And, therefore, how he's able to say what this is all about and whether he's correct in that assertion is a matter of his credibility. And therefore, as I pointed out yesterday when Mr. Zecevic gave him a date, he shouldn't be doing that because we say that this witness's ability to give evidence is not directly from his own knowledge, as he appears to be asserting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zecevic, you've heard Ms. Korner's concerns, and you will phrase your questions accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I understand. Can I establish with the witness whether he speaks English, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That would perhaps be useful, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you speak English, Mr. Tusevljak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't speak English. But very often when talking to persons from the international community when I presented certain matters to them and when we talked, very often I had to explain that I could not have tête-à-tête meetings with them for the simple reason that I do not speak their language. During my education for 12 years I studied Russian and I knew Russian very well, but I've forgotten that as well because I haven't been using it. So I don't understand English. I never attended any course whatsoever. So regardless of whether anyone believes it or not, I would sincerely be very happy if you were right, if I did understand or speak English, but I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document 65 ter 126D1. That is tab 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document sent to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to the commander personally, and it has to do with problems of the members of the Ilidza SSJB, and the date is the 23rd of November, 1992. In the signature it says "for CSB chief Zoran Cvijetic." Can you tell us whose signature this actually is?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you send this document to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, briefly, what is this about? What kind of problems concerning the members of the Ilidza SSJB did you want to inform the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This shows that in this document I am simply relaying the communication sent from the Ilidza SSJB. In it they say that they were mistreated by some units of the Army of Republika Srpska and that they're asking for that to be brought to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what was your request then to the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that it's only in the last paragraph that I say "please take action in line with the above document." I mean, I'm addressing those people from the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija corps. "And place the said formations under control so that similar situations do not arise in the future." And I'm asking them to get back to us with some information, however, referring to the number of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D587, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, this is a two-page document. So the first page is this letter signed by the witness and attached is the document or letter sent by the Ilidza Public Security Station. P842, tab 48, is the number of this attachment as a separate document. Could the witness please be shown 950D1, tab 174. Page 2, please, could we have that on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, before I put a question to you, after Borislav Maksimovic was replaced as chief of public security station of Vogosca, do you remember who was appointed chief of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zivko Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document before us is dated the 14th of December and it is a reply to a dispatch of the 11th of December. What is typewritten at the bottom is "chief of SJB Zivko Lazarevic." Can you tell us whether you have seen this document before and can you tell us what this document refers to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this document because, yet again, as you can see up here, it was sent to Drago Borovcanin. But it is evident that it has to do with what was happening in that area, in that part of the Sarajevo front line, and the chief of the public security station is informing the chief of the centre that the police is involved in combat. Also it is stated which policemen were wounded and also who engaged them in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, or, rather, can you give us an answer, or, rather, clarify this last thing that you said, "engaged them in the first place." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This shows that these policemen were engaged at -- upon an order from the Vogosca Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the witness testified he hadn't seen the document before. His answers about what it says are something that any reader would determine for themselves. In any event, what's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. I withdraw my proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on to a different subject matter now. Mr. Tusevljak, do you remember whether at some point in time during 1992 there was a vacancy advertised for admitting policemen into the MUP of Republika Srpska, and if so, when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that this was advertised but I really cannot remember exactly when it happened. I know that that was done because it was the crime police that was supposed to be manned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was it only the crime police that was supposed to be manned on the basis of this vacancy announcement, or other police departments too?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other police departments too. That's what I said -- meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since these documents haven't been translated yet, I'm going to skip this and perhaps I'll ask you on Monday about all of this. Sir, at the beginning of your testimony we looked at a report from the beginning of July from Vogosca that was written up by the operatives who had gone there to establish what the situation was. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In that document there was a proposal made by these operatives in their report, namely that Brane Vlaco be appointed chief of the crime police in Vogosca. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then I asked you about this gentleman and you gave us some information. Tell me, do you remember what his real name was? His first name?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branislav, I think. Branislav Vlaco. His full name. Brane is just a nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person with the same last name but a different first name, namely Branko Vlaco?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met that person sometime during the course of the war in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about this gentleman, Branko Vlaco?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a retired policeman and that at the beginning of the war he was prison warden, or sometime during 1992, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The warden of which prison?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A prison that was somewhere in the area Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, do you know, what the name of this prison was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact name of that prison. I know it was somewhere in Semizovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Trial Chamber, these are documents P1499, P1500.13.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document, tab 96 [as interpreted]. 683D1. Sir, the document is dated the 25th of May, 1992. It's the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Vogosca. It's an order. Tell me, did you know that there was a Crisis Staff in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know who headed this Crisis Staff, who was its president?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president was Jovan Tintor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us please look at paragraphs 1 and 3 of this order. In paragraph 1 it is ordered to put into operation the municipal court, the municipal misdemeanours court of the Serbian municipality of Vogosca, and to start resolving top priority cases in the areas of security, public law and order, and national defence. And in parentheses it says to be implemented by Zdravko Luketa. Tell me, do you know who Zdravko Luketa is?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never met the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the area of public law and order is under whose jurisdiction, according to the law?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember right now who established municipal misdemeanours courts and what their jurisdiction was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Public law and order, was that under the MUP, or, rather, the Ministry of the Interior, maintaining law and order?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, yes. That was one of the basic duties of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 says: "The public security station of the Serbian municipality of Vogosca is to be immediately put into operation and all necessary measures are to be taken to ensure that it functions properly." In parentheses it says: "To be implemented by Slavko Draskovic." Tell me, do you know who Slavko Draskovic is? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Slavko Draskovic. He was one of the top people in the CSB Sarajevo before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since this is the 25th of May, do you know whether Slavko Draskovic was a member of the MUP of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't know, whether he was a member of the MUP of Republika Srpska. More than a month had elapsed since the MUP was set up, so I really don't know whether he was a member at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Before hostilities broke out was there a public security station in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the public security stations in the territory of the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what is your understanding of this order, paragraph 3, to put into operation the public security station and to take measures to ensure that it functions properly?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absolutely not in accordance with the Law on the Interior, and the municipal authorities should not have anything to do with police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am aware of the fact that the witness said -- actually, I didn't even ask him, I just assumed that he hasn't seen the document before. But because of some of the other documents that we already have in evidence, I would like to tender this document, unless there are any objections by the Prosecutor. I can also provide appropriate references.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like you to adjourn that question until after the adjournment. There's something I need to check over the adjournment in respect of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break now, to return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can I say that in our earphones and on the screen was recorded tab 96, which caused some confusion because it isn't, it's tab 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it's tab 90 and I said tab 90.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, it came over as 96. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we rise today, I would require 10 minutes to inform the Trial Chamber of the schedulings of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have some information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we trust the extended break, which we didn't fully anticipate when we rose, was such that Ms. Korner has been able to complete the checks that she required in terms of the application to admit this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Ms. Korner was able to do it in five minutes and I've no objection to the document being exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D588, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak, let us take a look at document 684D1, tab 91. This is a document originating from the Crisis Staff in Vogosca. It's dated the day after, the 26th of May, 1992. It's an order signed by president of the justice department, Zdravko Luketa. And it's an order sent to the warden of the prison in Vogosca. First of all, tell me whether you have seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you do not know Zdravko Luketa.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of this document we see the following: "Twenty persons are left in the prison and are being operatively processed. Their well-being shall be the responsibility of the prison warden." Being operatively processed, are you aware that some individuals were being operatively processed in the prison in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 26th of May, 1992, we did not have crime prevention police in Vogosca, so I have no idea what this is supposed to mean, being operatively processed. I don't think that this was any operational processing. I think this is just a word game. The person writing the document probably thought that he was defining something while he wasn't. Operative work is work in the field, not work with some individuals. Anyway, there was no crime prevention police, which means that no operative work could have been conducted at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain the phrase "operative work," somebody being operatively processed within the framework of the crime prevention police, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You learn that a criminal offence was committed. You undertake certain operative measures and activities in order to shed light on this offence. This entails performing informative interviews in the field, carrying out certain checks in various registers, collecting all other information. This is the essence of operative work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this operative work carried out by the inspectors of crime prevention police?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mostly it's the inspectors of the crime prevention police. And also, within their domain, members of other services. If we are talking about criminal offences, then it is exclusively members of the crime prevention police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, when was the crime police department formed in the police station in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime towards the end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the document at hand. According to you, who was able to perform operative work on those 20 persons, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we find ourselves in the same situation as with the last document. This document together with another document tendered during the Prosecution case, P1494, makes a whole, so I propose to tender this document into evidence. I do agree that the issue of the nexus between this witness and this document is somewhat unresolved. Maybe I should first ask Ms. Korner whether she has any objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I didn't object because of the inquiries I made on the last occasion, but as Mr. Zecevic points out, some of these documents came in through a witness who was more qualified to deal with it than this one, and I'm not clear why a witness -- why a document that was disclosed in 2006 is being put to a witness who can't talk about it at all, other than to say he doesn't know what they mean by "operatives." And, as I say, I let the last document go in, and it's a matter for Your Honours if you think this is a proper way of dealing with it. But it does seem to me that the proper witness ought to have dealt with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We appreciate, Mr. Zecevic, your wishing to connect this with a document that's already in evidence, but we don't see how we can accede to the present application to admit it at this stage through this witness. So what we will do is mark it for identification pending either a better witness coming in or I suppose it may be left to become part of your bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Your Honours. I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D589 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 953D1, tab 161. Excuse me, 954D1, tab 162.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a bulletin by Serbia municipality of Vogosca, prison department, dated the 27th of September, 1992. It pertains to the 26th of September, 1992. It's signed by the prison warden Branko Vlaco, and we see a signature. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is a bulletin that had not been submitted to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at tabs 163, 164, and 165, documents 955D1, 956D1, and 957D1. Those are also bulletins pertaining to various dates, two from July and one from August. And then tell me whether you ever saw any of these bulletins. Was any of those bulletins sent to the Ministry of the Interior or, more precisely, to the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had nothing to do with this department. It was part of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska and I had no opportunity to see this or to know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, does the Ministry of the Interior have any jurisdiction, any authority, over the prisons or other places where prisoners are kept?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to show you another document. 960D1, tab 168. It is another document originating in the prison department in Vogosca. It's report on release of prisoners. It's dated the 9th of October, 1992, and it's signed by the prison warden Branko Vlaco. Sir, have you ever seen this report? Have you ever received this report in the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just like the previous documents, we haven't received this or any other similar reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was the chief of the public security station in Vogosca already replaced in October? I'm referring to Branislav Maksimovic. He was replaced by -- excuse me, I -- he was replaced by Zivko Lazarevic in the position of the chief of public security station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, yes. I think that the management personnel had already been replaced at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Public security stations -- or, rather, what are public security stations supposed to include in their daily reports sent to Security Services Centres?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports included, first of all, the situation at the front line relating to the engagement of police forces on the front line. All those police stations were in the territory of intense combat activities. After that there was a bulletin of events related to public law and order and also to criminal offences whose -- which had been detected. So those were the three main points in those daily bulletins. If there were any extraordinary events, they also would have been mentioned in the bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In case a criminal offence was committed and the perpetrator was arrested or detained, would this kind of information also be included in the daily report?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This kind of information would have been included in the daily report but also in a special dispatch sent to the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does the same go for the situation in which persons would be released from police detention?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was the police who made a decision on detention of three days, there would have been information on detention first. After that there should have been information on criminal reports submitted to the local prosecutor, and then it would depend on whether the prosecutor extended the detention or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that at some point in October 1992 you received a report from Vogosca relating to the fact that 11 individuals were released from detention?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 593D1, tab 172.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document originating in the Vogosca Brigade Command on the 17th September, 1992. It's addressed to the Vogosca Prison, attention of Brane Vlaco. Request 50 prisoners to work in the field. It's signed by Commander Trifunovic. Do you know this officer of the VRS named Trifunovic who belonged to the Vogosca Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that prisoners from the Vogosca Prison were taken out to work in the field? Do you have any information, operative information, did you learn anything from the report sent by the public security station in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received no information from the public security station in Vogosca about these kind of activities. They never reported anything similar to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to show you P1327, tab 100. Tab 100. Have you ever heard of the name Planja's House?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We didn't get a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in the war, only later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear during the war for Planja's House. Only later on when I was engaged in some other work did I find out about this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you were engaged in some other work, what exactly are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to my current job. I work in accordance with the guide-lines from the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the first day of your testimony when I posed questions about your career, I made an omission. I didn't ask you what is your current job. So I think this is a good opportunity for you to explain what you are currently doing.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm employed in the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. I'm co-ordinator for discovery and documenting of criminal offences related to war crimes. My job is to co-ordinate activities of the department for investigation of war crimes within the Republika Srpska MUP with the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina, district and cantonal prosecutor's office in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and other police agencies in Bosnia-Herzegovina involved in investigation of the aforementioned criminal offences, as well as the federal Ministry of the Interior. I also assist in investigations of those criminal offences conducted abroad. We had some cases in Norway, Sweden, United States, currently one in Great Britain, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With this decision, the Serbian municipality of Vogosca on the 8th of July, 1992, assigned the house of Almas and Miralem Planja in Semizovac for use to the Ministry of Justice. Were you aware of this at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the witness document 587D1. It is tab 169.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a decision, without a date though, signed by the minister of justice, Momcilo Mandic, and it says: "Decision. The detention department in Vogosca is hereby established as part of the Ilidza Butmir Penal and Correctional Facility. This decision will come into force on the day of issue." Tell me, first of all, are you familiar with the Butmir Correctional Facility in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That penal and correctional facility in Butmir in Ilidza, did it exist before the outbreak of conflict in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of penal and correctional facility was that Butmir facility in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a prison which was of the half-open type. That is to say, prisoners who had committed minor offences were sent to it. These were mostly traffic offences or crimes of economy or those who were prosecuted for misdemeanours and were sentenced with prison sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, do you know whether in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina what were the penal and correctional facilities in which persons served their sentences for more serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the penal and correctional facility in Foca, then the one in Zenica, in Doboj, and in Banja Luka. I think that these were the facilities for the most serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But we are talking about the period prior to the outbreak of conflict in April 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, these penal and correctional facilities, the four which you mentioned where persons served their sentences for more serious crimes, as well as the Butmir Penal and Correctional Facility, under whose jurisdiction had they been before the 1st of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And those who were located in the territory of Republika Srpska after the 1st of April, 1992, under whose jurisdiction were they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, during this morning's examination - though I'm not sure, as we have been talking for several days now - you mentioned that you know that in Vogosca there was a department of the prison and you mentioned a place or a name. Can you please repeat that for me? Where in Vogosca was that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in Semizovac, as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, could we ask that be spelled. Is that correct as it's come out on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Awhile ago I showed you a decision of the Serbian municipality in Vogosca on allocating Planja's House building to the Ministry of Justice, and the decision says that the house of Miralem and Almas Planja in Semizovac. Does that refer to the same place, Semizovac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the only place with that name in the territory of Vogosca municipality, and I think that there's even no other Semizovac in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that Momcilo Mandic was the minister of justice of Republika Srpska during 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would tender the document 587D1, tab 169, into evidence if there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, honestly, Your Honour, this could have been put to the witness himself when he gave evidence. This witness knows nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, perhaps the witness can take the -- his phones off. Your Honours, this document was found during the preparation of our Defence case in Sarajevo. It was located in the office of criminal support of defence teams for the State Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As Your Honours will surely recall, there was a case before the state criminal court, State Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina against Mr. Mandic and some other persons who were in charge of various detention facilities at the -- in the area of Sarajevo and so therefore we obtained this document only after the 1st of February this year and therefore were unable to present this document to Momcilo Mandic when he took the stand over here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, to contradict Mr. Zecevic, you'll see it's one of our documents. It's got an ERN number. Disclosed, batch 12, 2006 in response to a Rule 66 request. A Rule 66(B) request.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that fact. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Zecevic, what is this document to show?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is just to confirm that the -- that the Ministry of Justice actually established the correctional facility in Vogosca at Planja's House in Semizovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Before -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just say, Your Honour, I seem to recall - and I wasn't aware this application was going to be made, I thought this was more of this has got nothing to do with us - I have a feeling that Mr. Mandic was actually cross-examined about these matters and had something to say about it. And I don't know, I'd have to go back and check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Before we go to that, Mr. Zecevic, is your reading, and perhaps it's a translation issue, but is your reading that detention department being established means a detention centre? The detention -- first of all we didn't hear -- we didn't hear about what detention centre is meant here. You made a long way to come to Planja's House, but is this about Planja's House? And first of all, is what is said here in English, the detention department is hereby established, does that refer to detention centre or to a detention - I don't know - service? Offices? Perhaps it's more clear in the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid -- I'm afraid perhaps it needs an explanation. Every penal correctional facility has a part where the people who are sentenced are serving their sentence, and at the same time they have a part where the people who are in detention pending trial are kept. And according to our system, there is certain different rules which apply to one category, to the other category. Therefore, my reading of this document is that this refers to the establishment of the part of the KPD Butmir as a part for persons awaiting trial, and that is called the Department of Detention. That is my understanding. And I believe we have the evidence of Mr. Mandic to that respect, that it was actually situated in Planja's House, as we see from the document which I presented to Your Honours earlier on and witness commented on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document may be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D590, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us please now look at 1D339, which is tab 206.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, this is a decision of the Ministry of Justice dated the 21st of July, 1992, by which Branko Vlaco from Vogosca is appointed warden of the detention department of the Penal and Correctional Facility Butmir Ilidza located in Vogosca. It is signed by Avlijas. Do you know who Radomir Avlijas is? Excuse me, Slobodan Avlijas, rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can I ask where you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know who Slobodan Avlijas is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, maybe it's missing on the translation, but it says it's an illegible signature. And I'm just wondering how Mr. Zecevic is able to say it's Mr. Avlijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can clearly read the words which are written on the original, and it says Avlijas. And I don't think that was disputed before. This document is already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You say you know who Slobodan Avlijas is. Just tell me, where did he work in 1992 if you know, or, to be more specific, in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska, or the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at 1D189. It is tab 201. This is a document from the public security station in Vogosca dated the 12th of December, 1992, signed by the chief of the station, Zivko Lazarevic. It is a criminal report addressed to the military prosecutor's office in Sarajevo, Jahorina, in brackets, against Stanko Knezevic, and then his personal information is noted. Employed as a guardian in the Kula KPD Semizovac department, a Serb, et cetera, for the crime, as it is noted here, as there are reasonable grounds to suspect that --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, could we please move into private session now, and I will explain why. Can I ask that as a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For the final session today, we convene under Rule 15 bis, Judge Delvoie being absent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak, you were chief of the crime police of the CSB. Tell us, please, when a criminal report is filed to the prosecutor's office in charge, when that is done by the police, along with the criminal report, does one submit some attachments as well?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the evidence that was obtained in the pre-trial procedure, certificates of documents, reports, report from the site itself, and so on. Statements that were taken from various persons, that is to say, all the evidence that was gathered is an integral part of the criminal report, its attachments, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me -- just a moment, please. As a rule, when does the on-site investigation take place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, it is best to have it carried out as soon as possible, that is to say, immediately after the incident itself. However, if the situation does not permit that, then it can be done subsequently. The important thing is to secure the scene so that it is not compromised in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why is that important?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is important because the traces that can be found on the scene become evidence before a court of law against the person who is charged. Also, on the basis of the traces found, an unknown perpetrator is looked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, as time goes by, is it possible for the traces of a crime to disappear from the scene itself?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. As soon as it is compromised, it is compromised. And then other traces may be found, those that happened after the commission of the crime. And that may have destroyed the traces of the crime itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you mentioned reports, what reports do you mean? What kind of reports were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is the forensic report that is done by the crime technicians, the forensics people who deal with the traces found on the scene itself. If some expertise was carried out, then we also have expert reports.
